title: Queen against rook and pawn: the fortresses
summary: With an extra pawn, the rook sometimes draws against the queen. Which pawns hold, how to defend, and how the queen wins when there is no fortress.
part.fortress.title: The second-rank fortress
part.fortress.summary: Rook on a square the pawn protects, king beside it: the queen has nothing to do.
part.rules.title: Which pawns hold
part.rules.summary: A knight pawn almost always, a rook pawn on the third, a bishop or centre pawn on the second; from the third to the fifth, no.
part.rookPawn.title: Rook pawn on the second: no fortress
part.rookPawn.summary: Now with the queen: a rook with a single square falls to zugzwang, and an unprotected rook falls at once.
part.king.title: The king gets behind the pawn
part.king.summary: Against a bishop pawn on the third or fourth, the queen alone can't win: the king walks round and the pawn falls.
part.recap.title: Summary and Grigoriev's zugzwang
part.recap.summary: Three rules, the fortress with the pawn on the sixth, and the defence in the practical challenge.
step.t_fortress: Queen against rook and pawn. You have the rook and the pawn, and the queen looks far stronger. White to move. Before I explain, think: is there a way for White never to lose anything?
step.t_fortress.hint1: The f2 pawn protects two squares on the third rank. Find them, and see what happens if the queen takes the rook on one of them.
step.t_fortress.hint2: The rook only needs to go back and forth between those two squares, and the king stays glued to the pawn. The pawn never moves.
step.why: This is the fortress. The rook on e3 is protected by the pawn: if the queen takes it, fxe3 and only the kings are left. The third rank belongs to the rook, so the black king can't cross it. And our king has g1, h1 and h2 to escape the checks, always beside the pawn. Unable to get in or win anything, the queen can only check. Three conditions: the pawn protects the rook, the king protects the pawn, and the pawn stays put.
step.d_shuttle: Watch the rook go back and forth. I play both sides; notice that nothing changes, however hard the queen tries.
step.d_shuttle.m1: The rook goes to g3, the other square the pawn protects. A waiting move.
step.d_shuttle.m2: The black king goes to e4, hoping to come down to d3, behind our line.
step.d_shuttle.m3: But the rook returns to e3 with check: the third rank is hers.
step.d_shuttle.m4: The king steps back to f4.
step.d_shuttle.m5: And the rook goes back to g3. We are where we started.
step.d_shuttle.m6: The queen tries a check on the long diagonal.
step.d_shuttle.m7: The king goes to g1, next to the pawn. Not h3: the queen would mate on h1.
step.d_shuttle.m8: Another check, along the first rank.
step.d_shuttle.m9: And the king returns to g2. Two checks and nothing has changed: the queen has no way to improve.
step.shuttle: Now you defend. It's the same fortress with a centre pawn: the queen has just checked on d4. Block the check, answer the next check with the king beside the pawn and, when the black king reaches f4, switch the rook's square.
step.shuttle.hint: The rook has two good squares, d3 and f3. The king has two, d1 and d2, behind the rook.
step.shuttle.done: Rd3, Kd1 and, with the black king on f4, Rf3+ (Rh3 also holds): the rook switches protected square, and the other squares lose. The king goes back and forth between d1 and d2, behind the rook and beside the pawn, and the queen can check as long as it likes.
step.t_rules: Rook pawn on the third, rook on b2, king on b3. The black king is already on d3, very close. White to move. Only one move holds. Which?
step.t_rules.hint1: The rook can't leave b2: away from the king it falls, and Rb1 runs into Qc3+, with the black king backing it up.
step.t_rules.hint2: The king needs a square from which it keeps protecting the rook and gets no useful check. Think of the corner.
step.rulesTalk: Not every pawn makes a fortress. A pawn on the second rank, from b to g, with the rook on a square it protects: holds. A knight pawn, b or g: holds even on the fourth and fifth. A rook pawn: on the third, with the king in the corner. A bishop or centre pawn on the third, fourth or fifth: there is no fortress. Here, with the pawn on c3 and the rook on d4, White loses: the black king walks round and gets behind the pawn. On the sixth and seventh there is another fortress, with the rook behind the pawn, which depends on whose move it is: you'll see it at the end of the lesson.
step.knight: The knight pawn is the good exception. Pawn on b5, rook on c6 protected by it, king on b4 protecting the pawn: a draw. The queen has no room on the short side to attack from behind, and the rook shuttles between c6 and a6, the two squares the pawn protects.
step.corner: Now the rook pawn. Only one move holds; after it, shuttle the king between a1 and a2, and leave the rook on b2 while the black king is this close.
step.corner.hint: Get the king off the checking lines without abandoning the rook: the corner.
step.corner.done: Ka2, Ka1, Ka2, Ka1, Ka2. The king dances in the corner and the rook stays on b2. When the queen checks on d1, b1 also works for the rook, but the king in the corner is simplest.
step.t_rookPawn: Now you have the queen. Rook pawn on h7, rook on g6, the only square the pawn protects. White to play and win. Find the move that leaves Black without a good move.
step.t_rookPawn.hint1: Don't check. Think of a waiting move that leaves Black without a single good move.
step.t_rookPawn.hint2: The right square does two things at once: it watches the eighth rank and keeps the rook from leaving g6.
step.rookPawnWhy: Qe7, and it's zugzwang. The rook has only one protected square, g6: if it goes up to g7, Qe8 is mate; if it leaves along the sixth or down the g-file, it is unprotected and falls to a sequence of checks. The king only has h8, and there it is even worse off. With a rook pawn on the second rank the rook needed two squares and has only one.
step.d_zugzwang: Watch the zugzwang at work. The rook leaves, the queen checks, and the position comes back the same, with Black to move again.
step.d_zugzwang.m1: Qe7. No check: the queen watches e8 and f8 and pins the rook to g6.
step.d_zugzwang.m2: The rook goes to a6, as far as it can. Now it has no defender.
step.d_zugzwang.m3: Check along the eighth. The king only has f7 and g7.
step.d_zugzwang.m6: The king goes to h6, beside the pawn.
step.d_zugzwang.m7: Qc7. The queen waits, watching the seventh rank.
step.d_zugzwang.m8: The rook returns to g6 to cover.
step.d_zugzwang.m9: And the queen returns to e7. The same idea, with the black king worse off on h6, and Black to move: zugzwang again. Each cycle makes their position worse until the rook falls.
step.punish: Now the defender's other mistake. Here he pushed the pawn to f6, and the rook on e6 lost its protection. Punish it.
step.punish.done: Qxe6 (or Kxe6). The pawn that moved stopped protecting the rook. What's left is queen against pawn, and mate comes in a few moves.
step.t_king: Carlsen against Matlakov, 2019. Bishop pawn on the third, rook on d5, and the black king has left the pawn for c4. Our king is still far away. White to move. Find the move that leaves Black without a waiting move.
step.t_king.hint1: The black king can't leave the pawn, and the rook has to stay on the d-file to cut our king off. Which black piece still has waiting moves?
step.t_king.hint2: The queen needs to attack the pawn and, with the same move, watch the diagonal the rook would leave along.
step.kingWhy: A bishop or centre pawn on the third makes no fortress, but the queen alone can't win: every check gives the defender time to tidy the pieces again. The plan is to bring the king. Carlsen walked the king from h2 to e4 and then behind the pawn, while the queen drove the rook off its good squares. Once the king arrives, the rook runs out of squares, the pawn falls and what's left is queen against rook, which you already know how to win. It's a long road, but it's a win.
step.d_last: The end of Carlsen against Matlakov, 2019. The white king is already on c5, behind the pawn. Watch how the queen removes the pawn.
step.d_last.m1: Qf5. The queen attacks the rook on d3, which the king must keep protecting, and waits: Black has no good move.
step.d_last.m2: The king goes to c3, protecting the pawn and the rook.
step.d_last.m3: Check on the long diagonal. In the game the king went to b3, and the rook was left unprotected.
step.d_last.m5: Qf1. The queen attacks the rook on d3, which the king no longer protects.
step.d_last.m7: Qxc4+. The pawn is gone: queen against rook, and you know the rest.
step.zugzwang: Now you. Play the move that leaves Black without a waiting move.
step.zugzwang.hint: The queen goes to b6: it attacks c6 and eyes the diagonal down to d4.
step.zugzwang.done: Qb6, and Black has no waiting move: the rook checks, the king steps back, the pawn goes to c5 and the queen attacks it along the fifth rank. A few moves from now it falls.
step.summaryRules: To take with you: one, the fortress is a rook on a square the pawn protects, king beside it, and the pawn doesn't move. Two, a knight pawn almost always holds; a rook pawn, on the third; a bishop or centre pawn, on the second, and from the third to the fifth there is no fortress; on the sixth and seventh, with the rook behind the pawn, it depends on whose move it is. Three, with the queen, look for the zugzwang and bring the king behind the pawn; never just keep checking.
step.sixth: A different fortress, by Grigoriev, 1933: pawn on the sixth, rook behind it, king on c3. With Black to move it's a draw: the queen has no way to improve. With White to move, White loses: any move spoils it. It's a reciprocal zugzwang, which is why the king must reach c3 at the right moment.
step.grig: White to move. The king is on b3. Find the king square that makes the zugzwang Black's, then answer the check without abandoning the rook.
step.grig.hint: The square from which the king protects the rook and stands next to the pawn's file.
step.grig.done: Kc3 and, after the check on a1, the king goes to d2 (c2 and d3 also hold), close to the rook. It's Grigoriev's fortress: once the queen leaves the diagonal, the king returns to c3.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: hold the draw. Rook between e3 and g3, king glued to the pawn, and the pawn stays where it is.
key.fortress: The second-rank fortress, from Müller and Lamprecht (2001): rook on a square the pawn protects, king beside it. White to play and draw.
key.vdp: Van der Poel against Smits, 2000, with colours reversed: the same fortress with a centre pawn. The rook shuttles between d3 and f3 and the king between d1 and d2.
key.a3: Rook pawn on the third, from Schnabelwolke's study: only Ka2 holds, and the king stays in the corner.
key.b5: Knight pawn on the fifth, from Schnabelwolke's study: still a draw, because the queen has no room on the short side.
key.rook2: Rook pawn on the second, from KaushalK's study: the rook has only one protected square and Qe7 puts Black in zugzwang.
key.grigoriev: Grigoriev's reciprocal zugzwang (1933): pawn on the sixth, rook behind it. With Black to move, a draw; with White to move, a loss.
key.carlsen: Carlsen against Matlakov, Douglas 2019: a bishop pawn on the third makes no fortress. Qb6 is zugzwang.
history: Queen against rook without pawns is always a win. Give the rook an extra pawn and fortresses appear, and it took analysts a long time to map them. Nikolai Grigoriev published in 1933 the reciprocal zugzwang with the pawn on the sixth and the rook behind it. Karsten Müller and Frank Lamprecht, in Fundamental Chess Endings (2001), gave the rule of the second-rank fortress and the conditions under which it holds. Dvoretsky's manual devotes a section to the theme inside the queen-versus-rook chapter: the rook behind the pawn, the pawn on the seventh and on the sixth, the knight pawn on the fifth. In practice the ending fools even strong players. In 1959 Whitaker, with rook and pawn, claimed a draw against Ferriz in a position that was a win. In 1997, in Groningen, Vaganian only beat Bologan because both of them went wrong. In 2000, Smits held Van der Poel in the second-rank fortress. And in 2019, in Douglas, Carlsen showed Matlakov that a bishop pawn on the third makes no fortress: thirty moves of manoeuvring, the king behind the pawn, and the pawn fell.
practice: Now the practical challenge, with or without a clock. It's Müller and Lamprecht's fortress, and you defend: rook between e3 and g3, king beside the pawn, and don't touch the pawn.
ex.e01: White to move. The second-rank fortress, but Black has an extra pawn on h4. Hold the draw.
ex.e01.hint: The extra pawn takes away one of the rook's squares. Which one? And which one is left?
ex.e01.solution: Rh3 (Rf3+, Kg1, Kh2 and Kh3 also hold). Rg3 no longer works: hxg3 and the fortress is over. With the black pawn on h4 the rook only has e3 and h3, and the draw still stands.
ex.e02: White to move. Knight pawn on the fourth, rook on c4, unprotected. Find the move that keeps the fortress.
ex.e02.hint: The b4 pawn protects a5 and c5. The rook needs one of those squares.
ex.e02.solution: Rc5. The rook goes to the square the pawn protects, beside the king. Kc3 also holds, but leaves the rook on c4 for the queen to attack. A knight pawn on the fourth is still a fortress.
ex.e03: White to move. Marcotulli against Malström, 2001, with colours reversed. Bring the pieces to the knight-pawn fortress.
ex.e03.hint: Knight pawn on the fifth, rook on a square it protects, king beside the pawn.
ex.e03.solution: b5, Rc6 and Ka6 is the simple way: the pawn on the fifth, the rook on a square it protects and the king close by. Rook moves along the c-file also hold, because the pawn can advance later. In the game, the defender gave a rook check at the wrong moment and lost.
ex.e04: White to move. Knight pawn on the fourth, rook on c5 protected by the pawn, but the black king is right next to it. Which move holds?
ex.e04.hint: The rook can wait on the c-file, but not within the black king's reach.
ex.e04.solution: Rc8 (Rc7, Rc6, Rc1 and Kb6 also hold). The rook waits on the c-file, away from the black king; after the queen's waiting move it returns to c5. Rc3 loses at once to Kxc3, and Rc2 and Rc4 lose as well.
ex.e05: White to move. A position by G. Laza: rook pawn on the second, the rook on g6 and the black king in the corner. Force the rook in front of the king and close in with your king.
ex.e05.hint: Two checks force the rook in front of the king, and then our king steps in.
ex.e05.solution: Qf8+, Rg8 forced; Qf6+, Rg7 forced; and Kh6. The rook is pinned in front of the king and the mate on g7 can't be stopped.
ex.e06: White to move. Whitaker against Ferriz, 1959, with colours reversed. The rook on e6 is not protected by the pawn. Only one move wins.
ex.e06.hint: A check on the diagonal that reaches h7. Then another attack on the rook, with or without check.
ex.e06.solution: Qc2+. If Kg8, Qc8+ and Qxe6. If Kh6, h5! (Qd3 also wins): the pawn takes g6 from the black king, Kxh5 runs into mate in a few moves, and with no squares for the king the rook falls in the end. In the game, the side with the rook claimed a draw in a lost position.
ex.e07: White to move. Vaganian against Bologan, 1997. Queen against rook and a bishop pawn on the fourth. Only one move wins.
ex.e07.hint: Checks hand the fortress back to the defender. Bring the king closer.
ex.e07.solution: Kf4, the only move: the king heads for e3 and d3, behind the pawn. In the game Vaganian checked, let the fortress come back twice, and only won because Bologan made the last mistake.
ex.e08: White to move. The second-rank fortress is set up, but our king is already past the sixth rank. Only one move wins.
ex.e08.hint: With the king this close, the threat is mate. Start with a check along the eighth and bring the king to g7.
ex.e08.solution: Qb8+, Ke7 (the only move) and Kg7, threatening mate on f8. The rook has to leave, and the queen takes d8: the black king is stuck in front of its pawn and the pawn falls. With Black to move, Kc7 or Kc8 would draw.
ex.e09: White to play and draw. A study by Pogosyants: rook and pawn on the seventh against the queen, with the black king in front of the pawn.
ex.e09.hint: Check first, to drive the black king off c8. Then our king steps out of the pin, and the pawn promotes with check.
ex.e09.solution: Rc2+, Kd8; Kb8, so the pawn is no longer pinned; the queen goes to f5 and f8=Q+ forces the trade; then Rc8+ and the rook takes the queen. Rf2 on the second move also draws.
ex.e10: White to play and draw. A study by Prokeš: pawn on c7, rook on c8 and the black queen ready to check. Six moves, nearly all of them the only move.
ex.e10.hint: The rook goes to the one square from which, after the pawn is lost, it can still check all the way to stalemate.
ex.e10.solution: Rd8, then after the checks Kb7 and Ka8; when the queen takes on c7, Rd5+, Rb5+ and Rb6+: the black king has to take the rook and stalemates ours. Any other rook square on the first move loses the pawn without the trick.
